subject: computing
displayName: KS3 Computing — Variables, Data Types & Input/Output
subtitle: Storing data in variables, understanding data types, and handling user input and output.

data.targetWord: A named storage location in the computer's memory that holds a value which can change while the program is running

examples.en-GB: The variable 'score' holds the player's current score and updates each time they earn points.

data.targetWord: A named value that is set once at the start of a program and does not change during execution; written in UPPERCASE by convention

examples.en-GB: CONSTANT MAX_ATTEMPTS = 3 — this value never changes while the program runs.

data.targetWord: A whole-number data type with no decimal point; can be positive, negative, or zero

examples.en-GB: The values 42, -7, and 0 are all integers; they have no fractional part.

data.targetWord: A data type for numbers that include a decimal point (real numbers), used for measurements and averages

examples.en-GB: The value 3.14 is a float; it cannot be stored as an integer without losing precision.

data.targetWord: A data type that stores text — any sequence of characters enclosed in quotation marks

examples.en-GB: "Hello", "42", and "SW1A 1AA" are all strings because they are enclosed in quotation marks.

data.targetWord: A data type with only two possible values: True or False; used in conditions and logic

examples.en-GB: The expression age >= 18 evaluates to the Boolean True if age is 18 or more, and False otherwise.

data.targetWord: The operation of storing a value in a variable using the = operator in Python or ← in pseudocode

examples.en-GB: The statement score = 0 assigns the value 0 to the variable score.

data.targetWord: Explicitly converting a value from one data type to another, for example converting a string to an integer

examples.en-GB: int("42") uses type casting to convert the string "42" into the integer 42 so arithmetic can be performed.

data.targetWord: Data received into a program from the user, typically typed via the keyboard and stored in a variable

examples.en-GB: In Python, name = input("Enter your name: ") reads the user's keyboard entry and stores it.

data.targetWord: Data displayed from a program to the user, typically shown on screen using print() in Python or OUTPUT in pseudocode

examples.en-GB: print("Your score is:", score) sends the value of score to the screen as output.

data.targetWord: A classification that tells the computer what kind of value a variable holds and what operations can be performed on it

examples.en-GB: Knowing the data type of a variable matters: you can add two integers but cannot add an integer to a string without casting.

data.targetWord: The act of creating a variable and giving it a name, sometimes also assigning an initial value

examples.en-GB: Writing score = 0 at the start of a program is both a declaration and an initialisation of the variable.

data.targetWord: The name given to a variable, constant, or subroutine by the programmer; must be unique and meaningful

examples.en-GB: In the statement age = 14, the identifier is 'age' — the name used to refer to that memory location.

data.targetWord: The piece of data currently stored inside a variable or constant at a given moment during program execution

examples.en-GB: After score = 85, the value stored in the variable score is 85.

data.targetWord: A value or variable that an operator acts upon in an expression

examples.en-GB: In the expression score + 10, 'score' and '10' are the operands and '+' is the operator.

data.targetWord: The area inside the computer where data is temporarily stored while a program is running; variables occupy named locations in memory

examples.en-GB: When you create a variable, the computer reserves a location in memory and labels it with the variable's name.

data.targetWord: An agreed style for writing variable and constant names to make code consistent and readable across a codebase

examples.en-GB: A common naming convention for Python variables is snake_case, where words are separated by underscores: player_score.

data.targetWord: A Python function that converts a value to an integer data type; commonly used to cast user input from string to integer

examples.en-GB: int("42") converts the string "42" to the integer 42, making arithmetic possible.

data.targetWord: A Python function that converts a value to a string data type; used when joining numbers with text for output

examples.en-GB: str(99) converts the integer 99 to the string "99" so it can be joined with other text using +.

data.targetWord: A Python function that converts a value to a float data type; used when decimal precision is required from user input

examples.en-GB: float("3.14") converts the string "3.14" to the float 3.14 so it can be used in calculations.

data.targetWord: A pseudocode keyword that reads data entered by the user from the keyboard and stores it in a variable

examples.en-GB: name ← USERINPUT pauses the program and waits for the user to type something, then stores it in 'name'.

data.targetWord: The Python function used to display output to the user on screen; equivalent to OUTPUT in pseudocode

examples.en-GB: print("Hello, World!") sends the text Hello, World! to the screen.

data.targetWord: A pseudocode keyword that displays data to the user; equivalent to print() in Python

examples.en-GB: OUTPUT "Well done, " + name displays a greeting message on screen in pseudocode programs.

data.targetWord: A naming convention where the first word is lowercase and each subsequent word starts with an uppercase letter, with no spaces

examples.en-GB: playerScore, firstName, and numberOfLives are all written in camelCase naming convention.

data.targetWord: A naming convention where all letters are lowercase and words are separated by underscores; commonly used in Python

examples.en-GB: player_score, first_name, and number_of_lives are all written in snake_case naming convention.

data.targetWord: The region of a program in which a variable exists and can be accessed; variables created inside subroutines have local scope

examples.en-GB: A variable declared in a function has local scope — it cannot be read or changed from outside that function.

data.targetWord: Setting a variable's first value at the start of a program or before it is used for the first time

examples.en-GB: Writing score = 0 at the start of a game initialises the score variable so it is ready to be updated.

data.targetWord: A fixed value written directly into the source code, such as the number 42 or the text "Hello"

examples.en-GB: In score = 100, the number 100 is a literal — it is a fixed value typed directly into the code.

data.targetWord: A combination of values, variables, and operators that the computer evaluates to produce a single result

examples.en-GB: score + 10 is an expression; when score is 85, the expression evaluates to 95.

data.targetWord: A single instruction in a program that performs one action, such as an assignment, a print, or an if condition

examples.en-GB: name = input("Enter your name: ") is a statement — it is one complete instruction that the program executes.

data.sentence: A variable is a named storage location in ____ that holds a value which can change while the program runs.
The value "Hello" has the data type ____.
The value 42 has the data type ____.
The value 3.14 has the data type ____.
The value True has the data type ____.
In Python, the = symbol is the ____ operator, not a test of equality.
To test whether two values are equal in Python, you use the ____ operator.
int("25") converts the string "25" to the ____ 25.
str(99) converts the integer 99 to the ____ "99".
float("3.14") converts the string "3.14" to the ____ 3.14.
In Python, input() always returns a value of type ____.
The pseudocode keyword used to read data from the user is ____.
The pseudocode keyword used to display data to the user is ____.
A constant is different from a variable because its value cannot ____ during the program's execution.
By convention, constant names are written in ____ to distinguish them from variables.
After the statement age = int(input("Age: ")), the variable age has data type ____.
The variable name my_score uses the ____ naming convention.
The variable name playerScore uses the ____ naming convention.
The value "3" enclosed in quotes is a ____, not an integer.
Converting one data type to another is called type ____.

data.title: Steps: Program that inputs name and age then outputs a greeting
data.instruction: Put the steps of this program in the correct order.
items: Display a prompt asking the user for their name
Read the user's name using USERINPUT and store it in a variable
Display a prompt asking the user for their age
Read the user's age using USERINPUT and cast it to an integer
Build the greeting string by joining the name and age variables with text
OUTPUT the greeting to the screen

data.title: Steps: Fixing a type error when adding string and integer
data.instruction: Put the debugging steps in the correct order.
items: Identify the line that causes the error — a string and integer are being added
Recognise that input() always returns a string in Python
Choose the correct cast function: int() to convert the string to an integer
Wrap the input() call with int() to convert the value before storing it
Rerun the program to confirm the type error no longer occurs
